There is a particular kind of silence that only exists at 3 a.m. in an empty kitchen. The refrigerator hums, low and faithful, the only thing awake besides you. Moonlight lays a cold rectangle across the linoleum, and the faucet drips once every seven seconds if you count. It is in this silence that your brain finally stops performing.

During the day we are curators of ourselves. We choose words, iron shirts, answer emails with exclamation marks to seem friendly. We nod. We carry our phones like talismans against boredom. But at 3 a.m., none of that matters. The performance has closed. The theater is dark.

I used to hate insomnia for stealing my mornings. Now I think it was giving me something rare: unobserved time. No one wants anything from you at 3 a.m. No one expects a reply. You can sit in socks that don't match and think unfinished thoughts without needing to make them clever for someone else.

Maybe this is why we love deserts, deep oceans, empty chapels. Not because they are beautiful, though they are, but because they offer the same unobserved feeling on a larger scale. A reminder that the world exists without an audience. That you do too.

And so I pour a glass of water I don't really need, just to break the silence gently, and go back to bed. Outside, the refrigerator keeps humming, keeping watch until morning finally asks me to perform again. I will be ready. But not just yet. Good night.
